messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Workplace: Workplace
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Vignette:
Mara was seventy-five years old, a retired auditor who had spent forty years in the same cubicle, and she had never expected to be afraid of her own living room. She had been born on a small island in the Pacific, raised by her grandmother in a house that smelled of salt and frangipani, and had moved to the mainland as a young woman for a job she never quite loved but never left. She had been married to a quiet, steady man named Tomas for fifty-two years, and they had raised three children in a suburban house with a fenced yard. Then, at sixty-eight, she had gone back to visit her grandmother’s village during a period of political instability that the news called a civil conflict, and she had been caught in a market square when a shell hit the building next to the fruit stalls. She had not been injured, not physically, but she had been pinned under a collapsed awning for three hours, surrounded by the smell of sweat and blood and overripe mangoes, listening to a woman scream until the screaming stopped. She had not spoken of it much afterward. She had returned home, returned to her spreadsheets and her grandchildren’s birthday parties, and told herself she was fine.

The trouble began quietly. At first, it was only that she noticed she could not find the words when someone asked about the trip. She knew exactly what had happened—she could see it in her mind as clearly as a photograph, the way the dust had settled on the dead woman’s hair, the angle of a broken chair leg, the pattern of light through the ripped awning—but when she tried to describe it, her mouth went dry and her throat closed and she ended up saying, “It was loud,” or “It was very hot.” She stopped trying. Then the smells started coming back unbidden, the thick, sour scent of sweat and body odour from the people pressed against her under the awning, and she would be standing at the grocery store and suddenly gag, unable to explain to the cashier why she had to leave. She began to avoid the produce section in summer.

Over the months, her world shrank. She had always been a woman who sat with her back to the room, comfortable in her own home, but now she could not bear it. She rearranged the furniture in the den so that her armchair faced the door, and she insisted on sitting with her back against the wall in restaurants, even if it meant turning down invitations from friends. She started checking behind her when she walked to the mailbox, a quick, furtive glance over her shoulder that she tried to pass off as looking for a neighbour’s cat. Tomas noticed, but when he asked, she said she was just getting old and cautious. She began to rehearse conversations before she had them, running through what she would say to the pharmacist, to her daughter on the phone, to the man who delivered their groceries, because she had come to believe that if she said the wrong thing, people would see it. She was certain that others could look at her and know what had happened, that the fear was written on her face like a scar, and the only way to hide it was to control every word.

She started taking risks she had never taken before. She drove through red lights at three in the morning because she was convinced someone was following her, and she needed to lose them. She walked alone through a dangerous part of town at dusk because the direct route home required crossing a parking lot with her back exposed, and that felt worse. She knew, in a distant, logical part of her mind, that this was dangerous, but the danger of the street felt smaller than the danger of being trapped. And she ruminated. She lay awake at night, going over and over why this had happened to her, what she could have done differently, whether she should have stayed home, whether she should have run faster, whether the woman who had screamed might have survived if Mara had done something, anything. She could not stop the loop. She began to feel that she would never feel normal again, that the part of her that had once laughed at her grandchildren’s jokes or enjoyed a quiet evening with Tomas was gone, replaced by a hollow vigilance. She told herself that her life was not worth living if this was all that was left, but she did not say it aloud.

What finally brought her to a therapist was the workplace trigger. She had been retired for a decade, but her daughter had asked her to help with the books at a small nonprofit, just a few hours a week. The office smelled like old coffee and stale air, and the fluorescent lights hummed, and within three days Mara could not go back. The smell of the building—the particular sour warmth of unwashed bodies in a closed space—had unlocked something, and she had stood in the supply closet shaking, unable to breathe, unable to find the words to tell her daughter why she was leaving. She called a clinic the next morning. She said, “I need help,” and then she could not say anything else.
